Thank you for submitting your work entitled “Normative evidence accumulation in unpredictable environments” for peer review at eLife. Your submission has been favorably evaluated by Timothy Behrens (Senior and Reviewing Editor) and three peer reviewers.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

The study of how the brain integrates a history of evidence into a single expectation has been a remarkably profitable avenue of research in forming quantitative understandings of neural mechanisms over recent years and decades. However, two largely distinct literatures have tackled this problem from very different perspectives. One set of researchers have considered the mathematics and neurophysiology of integrating continuous streams of evidence using approaches such as the drift diffusion model and the sequential probability ratio test. Another set of researchers have considered the integration of discrete events or trials using Bayesian models that can, for example, optimally determine when to integrate evidence together, and when to separate new evidence because the world has changed.

The current paper presents an important step towards a unification of these two literatures, by presenting an elegant mathematical analysis of the Bayesian change-point models to demonstrate that they can be viewed as modified sequential probability ratio tests, and are therefore directly applicable to the large set of researchers who are interested in continuous evidence integration. It makes new and interesting predictions about the stream integration case in situations when the evidence is non-stationary and it tests these predictions in behaviour. All three reviewers considered this to be a very interesting and potentially important step.

As you will see below, the reviewers did not have major criticisms of the model that is presented or data, which they broadly found to be convincing. Most important in terms of solidifying the conclusions, however, are Reviewer 1's and 3's similar points about the demonstration of the qualitative reason for the improvement of the current model (Reviewer 1) and the absence of a reasonable analysis of other (sub-optimal) models (Reviewer 3).

In the discussion, the reviewers and editor were also clear that the manuscript is really written for a technical audience. eLife readership is broad and the reviewers and editor would appreciate a reframing of the paper that makes the central points clearer to this broad audience.

One suggestion that emerged during the discussion was a clearer framing of the manuscript as follows:

a) The same Bayesian learning framework, that has been used in other contexts (work by Behrens, Adams, Kording and also Nassar and Gold) is here derived for evidence accumulation in perceptual decision-making tasks like RDM;

b) This normative framework can be described, in both discrete and continuous cases, as a leaky accumulator with non-absorbing bounds, with the leak rate and the height of the bounds being explicit functions of the environmental change rate;

c) Show that this is the case in their data (their paradigm with variable hazard rate is a good test even if atypical of RDM experiments);

d) Provide some justification why this model helps our understanding of perceptual decision-making (can the relationship with change point detection explain or offer insight into previously unexplained data?);

e) Provide some clear commentary on the relationship to previous models of change point detection (can the relationship with RDMs explain or offer insight into previously unexplained data?).

We urge you to consider this, or other possible reframings in which the strong message can be understood clearly without an understanding of the technical details.

Reviewer #1:

In this study, Glaze, Kable and Gold present a model of evidence integration over time in which the relative weighting given to new and past observations can be adjusted to reflect the hazard rate for change in the environment. They show that this model can be generalized to both discrete and continuous time cases and that it fits human performance better than a model without adjustable hazard rate, in two very different decision-making tasks – a random dot motion task with within-trial reversals, and a task in which evidence is accumulated over many discrete trials.

This is a good quality paper which I think will be of interest to people across the field of perceptual decision-making, since it presents a clear framework that is applicable in diverse tasks. It could be an influential and highly cited paper in the field.

If I were to make a case why the manuscript should be published in eLife, I would point out that the adaptation of the Bayesian framework to the random dot motion case does represent a major conceptual advance over the more typical approaches in that field (SPRT models with fixed leak rates or the drift diffusion model), and the model does better at explaining participants' performance than those more typical models. However, I would then suggest that the paper could be strengthened by exploring in more detail why the current model outperforms others (especially, the leaky accumulator with hazard rate as a free parameter by block). Is this because the leaky accumulator down weights past beliefs about the correct response without taking into account evidence strength? If so the reason for the current model's superiority is not really to do with estimating the hazard rate, although the text implies that it is. Furthermore, to what extent does the current model address burning questions in that field, such as how confidence judgements are made or when the evidence accumulation process should terminate?

Reviewer #2:

In this manuscript by Glaze et al., the authors present a normative model for evidence accumulation in a non-stationary environment in which the successive simples are drawn from one of two alternative distributions for an unknown and variable duration. The main part of the manuscript is to compare the performance of human subjects in two different behavioral tasks with the predictions of this normative model and a simpler alternative model based on leaky integration. The results show that human subjects differ significantly from the predictions of normative model, in that subjective estimate of the rate of change (hazard rate) is close to 0.5, suggesting that they tend to give insufficient weight to the history of evidence. Although the manuscript is quite technical in nature, it is written clearly, and the findings would be of high value to many researchers in the field. There are only a few, relatively minor, comments:

1) The overall conclusion of the authors is that the subjective estimates of hazard rate are biased, but this quantity is used in a normative way. However, this might be misleading. Namely, is it fair to refer to an algorithm as “normative” if the quantity used in this algorithm is biased? Does such an algorithm behave differently, for example, from a model that uses the accurate estimate of hazard rate in non-normative way? Unless the authors can clarify how these two different scenarios can be distinguished, how the word “normative” is used in this manuscript might need to be improved.

2) In the subsection “Psychophysics”, the authors should indicate for how many sessions, trial-by-trial feedback was provided in the beginning and end of each block.

3) What do green and blue colors in Figure 7A indicate?

Reviewer #3:

This is an interesting paper that provides a significant contribution through the clear derivation of a normative approach for accumulation of evidence under conditions where the evidence is not stationary. The derivation and the description of how changes in the rate of change of environments correspond to leakiness in accumulation was very appealing.

I found the experimental section convincing in terms of showing that humans do indeed try to estimate the rate of change of the environment, and that this estimate affects how they make decisions. But the further claim made in the paper that humans behave according to the normative model was harder to be convinced by – it seemed that other (suboptimal) models that use an estimate of the hazard rate might also be consistent with the data, but this wasn't much explored in the paper. Instead, the straw man such as a model where the estimated hazard rate is a single value fixed for all time was used, but it seemed rather a weak straw man.

In addition, much greater clarity in the exposition would be desirable.

Despite these concerns, the nice derivation of the normative results under changes in environments makes me see the paper positively.

claims.claim: Standard sequential-sampling models are normative only when the ideal starting time-point for accumulation is known.
claims.source: These models have been useful for studying neural mechanisms of decision-making (Gold and Shadlen, 2007) but are normative for only a restricted set of conditions in which: (1) the ideal starting time-point for accumulation is known (e.g., given by the onset of an experimental trial); and (2) the statistics of the incoming information are perfectly stable throughout the entire sequence, with no change in the underlying signal and all noise coming from the same probability distribution.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing models with citation support.

claims.claim: Standard sequential-sampling models are normative only when the statistics of the incoming information are perfectly stable throughout the entire sequence.

claims.evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing models with citation support.

results.result: The authors derived a novel normative model for decision-making in unstable environments based on Bayesian principles. The model defines belief as log posterior odds and updates it based on sensory evidence (LLR) and a prior expectation (ψ) that depends on hazard rate H. For H=0 (perfect stability), the model reduces to perfect accumulation; for H=0.5, history is irrelevant; for high H, accumulation is limited to facilitate change detection.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C11-C19 collectively establish the theoretical foundation of the normative model with clear mathematical definitions and limiting cases. The derivation is based on established Bayesian principles (C11) with appropriate citations, and the special cases (C17, C18, C19) provide internal consistency checks. The model formulation is mathematically sound and well-justified.

results.result: The normative model exhibits two key dynamical regimes: (1) when beliefs are uncertain (L≈0), it acts as a leaky accumulator with leak rate directly dependent on H; (2) when beliefs are certain (|L|>>0), it approaches a stabilizing boundary whose height depends on H. This boundary suspends but does not terminate accumulation, unlike absorbing boundaries in traditional models.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C28 describe the model's key dynamical properties with appropriate mathematical approximations (Equation 3) and contrasts with existing models. The characterization of two regimes is well-supported by the mathematical derivations and figures (Figures 1B, 2A,C). The distinction from traditional models (C26, C28) is clearly articulated with citations.

results.result: The normative model predicts a trade-off between identifying steady signals and detecting changes that depends on both evidence strength and expected hazard rate H. For weak evidence, the trade-off is most severe, with the model optimizing for either change detection (high H) or signal identification (low H). As evidence strength increases, performance improves for both conditions and the trade-off diminishes.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C31 describe a key prediction of the model that is well-supported by the mathematical framework and illustrated in Figure 2E,G. This trade-off is a natural consequence of the model's dynamics and represents a testable prediction that is later validated in the empirical sections.

results.result: The authors developed a continuous-time version of the model based on optimal filtering for Markov jump processes. For λ=0, it reduces to perfect integration; for L≈0, it becomes an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process (leaky integration).
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C34 establish the continuous-time formulation with appropriate citations to the mathematical literature (Zakai, Liptser & Shiryaev, Crisan & Rozovskii). The limiting cases provide consistency checks analogous to the discrete-time model. The derivation appears mathematically sound.

results.result: In the triangles task, subjects adapted to different hazard rates, with subjective H estimates strongly correlated with objective H (r=0.721, p<0.0001). However, subjects systematically misestimated extreme hazard rates, with estimates tending toward H≈0.5. The normative model provided good fits to choice data (McFadden's r²=0.895±0.016) and outperformed a block-independent model (ΔBIC=-23.721±9.671, p<0.0001).
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C49 provide strong statistical evidence for learning and use of hazard rates in the triangles task. The correlation between subjective and objective H (C46), the regression slopes (C47), and model comparison statistics (C43) are all well-documented. The systematic bias toward H≈0.5 (C48, C49) is an important finding that persisted even with extended learning, suggesting a genuine cognitive constraint rather than insufficient experience.

results.result: In the triangles task, subjects' choice dynamics reflected key predictions of the normative model: (1) hazard-dependent biases when certainty was high (Spearman's r=0.890, p<0.0001); (2) hazard-dependent leak patterns including damped oscillations for high H; (3) a strong trade-off between change detection and steady signal identification that depended on both hazard rate and evidence strength, with the trade-off most severe for weak evidence.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C56 demonstrate that subjects' behavior matched specific qualitative predictions of the normative model. The hazard-dependent biases (C50), leak patterns (C51), and trade-offs (C53-C56) are all supported by statistical tests and figures. The control analysis showing that the block-independent model did not predict these dynamics (C52) strengthens the interpretation that subjects were using learned hazard rates.

results.result: Direct estimates of the mapping from beliefs to priors in the triangles task matched normative model predictions for all H-groups (Hotelling's t-test, p>0.05 for all groups). Two suboptimal models—a leaky accumulator without stabilizing boundaries and a perfect accumulator with stabilizing boundaries—provided worse fits than the normative model (34/48 subjects for both, p<0.0001 and p=0.007 respectively) and failed to capture key aspects of the data.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C62 provide strong evidence that the full normative model (with both leak and boundary) better describes human behavior than simpler alternatives. The direct estimation of belief-to-prior mappings (C57, C58) and the model comparison statistics (C59, C61) are well-documented. The specific failures of each suboptimal model (C60, C62) are identified with appropriate statistical tests.

results.result: In the dots-reversal task, subjects adapted to different hazard rates, with 12/13 subjects showing appropriate sensitivity to objective λ (p<0.05). The normative model performed well (McFadden's r²=0.385±0.055) and outperformed a block-independent model (ΔBIC=-4.790±1.216, p<0.0005). However, like in the triangles task, subjects systematically overestimated low values and underestimated high values of λ.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C70 demonstrate learning and adaptation in the dots-reversal task with appropriate statistical evidence. The model fit quality (C68) and comparison to the block-independent model (C67) are well-documented. The systematic bias in hazard rate estimation (C70) replicates the finding from the triangles task, strengthening the conclusion that this is a general feature of human learning in these contexts.

results.result: In the dots-reversal task, choice dynamics reflected normative model predictions: for high-coherence trials, strong evidence dominated with >90% accuracy within 500ms regardless of hazard rate; for low-coherence trials, integration times were strongly hazard-dependent, with accuracy worse for low-hazard conditions immediately after change-points (7.1±11.1% vs 40.3±2.8%, p<0.01) but better at longer durations (83.6±3.6% vs 69.9±8.3%, p<0.0005).
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C76 demonstrate the predicted trade-off between change detection and signal identification in the dots-reversal task. The statistical evidence is strong, with appropriate tests and error bars. The pattern of results—strong evidence dominates regardless of hazard rate (C71), while weak evidence shows hazard-dependent dynamics (C72-C75)—matches the normative model's predictions and parallels findings from the triangles task.

results.result: Direct measurement of leak dependence in the dots-reversal task showed that best-fitting leaks depended on both hazard rate (p<0.0005) and motion coherence (p<0.0001), with pairwise differences not differing from normative model predictions (p>0.05 for both comparisons). The normative model outperformed both a leaky-integrator model (10/13 subjects, p<0.05) and a bounded-accumulator model (9/13 subjects, p<0.05).
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C80 provide strong evidence that the full normative model captures the joint dependence of leak on both hazard rate and evidence strength. The statistical tests are appropriate, and the model comparisons demonstrate that both components (leak and boundary) are necessary to fully account for the data. The consistency with normative predictions (C78) is particularly compelling.

results.result: The authors establish the context and motivation for their work by noting that while normative models exist for learning in dynamic environments, they have not been applied to faster decision processes. Standard sequential-sampling models (SPRT, drift-diffusion) are normative only under restricted conditions (known start time, perfect stability), and perfect integration can be problematic for detecting signal changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C6-C10 establish the background and motivation with appropriate citations to the literature. The characterization of existing models and their limitations is accurate and well-supported by citations. This provides clear justification for the novel contribution of the current work.

results.result: The triangles task required 48 subjects to make trial-by-trial choices about which of two triangles generated a star position, with the correct source changing at a hazard rate that was constant within blocks but varied across blocks (0.05-0.95). Subjects were never instructed about hazard rates. In a subset of sessions, learning was facilitated with trial-by-trial feedback at the beginning and end of blocks.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C42, C95 provide a clear description of the triangles task design. The task is well-designed to test the model's predictions, with appropriate manipulation of hazard rates and control over feedback. The sample size (48 subjects) is reasonable for this type of study.

results.result: The dots-reversal task was a novel version of the random-dot motion task in which 13 subjects judged the final direction of motion after within-trial direction changes occurring at either 0.1 Hz or 2.0 Hz. Motion coherence was fixed within trials at either high or low values, and subjects received feedback after each trial.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66, C96 provide a clear description of the dots-reversal task design. The task is well-designed to test the model on a different timescale (within-trial vs. across-trial accumulation) and with different stimulus properties. The sample size (13 subjects) is smaller than the triangles task but reasonable given the within-subject design with multiple trials per condition.

results.result: The authors derived a normative model based on Bayesian principles for inferring changes in generative processes, incorporating change detection into sequential-sampling decision models. Unlike previous models, this formulation casts adaptation directly in the context of evidence accumulation. Human subjects made decisions on two tasks consistent with the model's adaptive, hazard-dependent accumulation process, learning hazard rates imperfectly but using them normatively.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C86 summarize the main contributions and findings of the work. These claims are well-supported by the detailed theoretical development and empirical results presented in earlier sections. The characterization of the model's novelty (C82, C83) is accurate, and the summary of empirical findings (C84-C86) is consistent with the detailed results.

results.result: The authors propose that deviations from optimality in human decisions can be interpreted as different hazard-dependent set-points of an inherent trade-off between sensitivity to change and steady-state signals. They speculate that prior expectations about environmental instability might provide new insights into previous findings of leaky accumulation, urgency signals, and other deviations from perfect integration, which might reflect normative adjustments to expected instabilities rather than computational limitations.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C93 present interpretations and speculations about the broader implications of the findings. While the framework for interpreting deviations from optimality (C87) is well-supported by the current results, the speculations about reinterpreting previous findings (C88-C93) are not directly tested in this work. These are reasonable hypotheses that would require additional empirical work to validate.

results.result: In the normative model, the adaptive accumulation process can be suspended by the non-linear dynamics of the accumulation process itself, not by an extrinsically imposed decision rule like an absorbing decision boundary, potentially providing a new perspective on speed-accuracy trade-offs.
results.evaluation: Claim C94 highlights an important conceptual distinction between the normative model and traditional sequential-sampling models. This is well-supported by the mathematical development showing how the stabilizing boundary emerges from the model's dynamics rather than being imposed externally. However, the implications for speed-accuracy trade-offs are speculative and not directly tested.
